page.title: The Perfect Input System
page.description: The Perfect Input System -- what KDE should do

content.p: Input subsystems don't always a lot of attention. We want them to just work, and they usually do, until the requirements get a little unusual.

One of the downsides of the Wayland system was that it unified the input system with the compositor, rather than having a separate one like X11's XInput. This has meant that they have often languished.
My goal here is to suggest some terminology (and possibly an object and configuration model?) that will help KDE and others cope with all the scenarios.
In the following scenarios, we have two habitual users of the computer, Bob and Alice. Each can log in on a separate seat, and has their own hardware, as follows:

ul.li: Mice: Just one, a Logitech G600 that has a built-in keyboard.
A lovely clicky keyboard, with a standard US layout
An OK keyboard, with a US-International layout, and a Russian layout
A cheap keyboard with both Greek and Hebrew layouts. It's the only one with Media keys

content.p: Bob's friend Ted is dropping by, and they expect to play Game X. Game X is designed for two users using the same screen. Bob hasn't yet bought and gaming devices, so each will be using a separate keyboard. Fortunately, Bob has 3 keyboards attached.

Bob's wife, Alice, wants to get the taxes done. She has, attached to the same computer, her own keyboard and mouse, and two screens, one for GnuCash, and one for the other things she'll be looking at while doing this.
The computer hosts two seats: seat0 and seat1.
seat0 belongs to Bob, who is logged in as a system user. It has one head (Bob’s display) and three keyboards attached.

ul.li: Two of these keyboards form Bob’s primary input set, used for everyday interaction.
The third keyboard belongs to a co-seat — a cooperative sub-arrangement within the same seat. This co-seat is used by Ted, a local participant sharing Bob’s screen and session during a game (GameX).
Ted does not have a separate system account or session; he operates through Bob’s session using his own input device.

content.p: seat1 belongs to Alice, who is logged in independently. It has its two heads (display) and a single keyboard. Alice’s session and input devices are entirely separate from Bob’s.

tr.td: Standard US, comfortable (Cheery MX blue keys)

ul.li: A seat is a grouping of input and output devices that form a complete interactive workstation.

A sub-seat is a cooperative subdivision of a seat, used when two or more participants share the same seat’s head(s) but operate through distinct input devices. These are divided into master seats (one per seat) and co-seats, of which there can be multiple per seat.
A head is a display output associated with a seat.
Each user runs one session per seat.
In this configuration, Bob and Ted share a session through a co-seat; Alice runs independently on her own seat and session.

tr.td: Each seat has its own display and associated input devices.
Cooperative subset of a seat’s inputs
“GameX co-seat” assigned to Ted within Bob’s session

content.p: That's all well and good, but let's try another scenario.
content.h1: 🖥️ Scenario 2: Alice and Bob with Multiple Input Devices
content.p: Now Alice and Bob, with the same physical hardware configuration, are doing new tasks. Alice, an introvert, is playing a game by herself. Bob is working on his language teaching books. There are no co-seats; each seat has only one sub-seat.
Alice doesn't need to do anything from an Input System point of view. Bob needs to change his seat configuration to not have a co-seat.

However, Bob will be regularly switching between US International+Greek and Hebrew+Russian layouts. This needs to be changed at a seat level. Fortunately, in this ideal layout, instead of switching keyboard layouts, one can also switch seat configurations. Bob has hotkeys for his favourite seat configurations.

At this point, it's instructive to go back and look at the Hardware Mapping table. Note that the standard US keyboard and the G600 keyboard are part of the same virtual keyboard. This will be the same across all seat configurations.
The mouse situation is similarly complex; imagine a computer with a standard mouse or two, a graphics tablet (eg. the Wacom ones), and a SpaceNavigator.

Bob has finished his Greek/English book, and his Russian/Hebrew book. Now he's writing a new book about his experiences, and it involves all 4 languages. So he wants to be able to switch keyboard layouts independently. He creates one seat layout in which the two virtual keyboards each switch layout independently, meaning he can access the approriate language on each keyboard easily.
Bob gets a new laptop for work. Work provides him with 2 screens at work, and he picks up 3 second-hand monitors at home.

As a general rule, Bob wants one screen for his terminal windows/code (portrait mode), one screen for his AI, and one or two screens for the other things he's working on (in web browsers). In the past, when he went from work to home, his windows would all end up on the wrong screens. However, this new setup allows not just for multiple heads, but for named heads. So he can have two seat configurations, one for work and one for home. But since his heads have the same names ("Terminal", "AI", "Web 1", and optionally "Web 2"), so his windows all get restored to the correct screens.
So, from a Seat Configuration point of view, we have:
